🗒️What This Means For You
  • Fed Hike: Since the 2026-09-16 Fed hike the Treasury-rate leg of IG returns is -1.68% (intraday, 7-year +24bp). At trading day 9 (last close) it was -1.35% against a five-campaign average of -0.34% at the same point — only 2022-23 was worse. The spread leg adds -0.35%. The 10-year is +26bp since the hike vs a +4bp campaign average at the same point.
  • Stocks: The Dow and S&P slipped, but the tech-heavy Nasdaq still closed higher.
  • FX: The dollar barely moved; the euro and yen were flat against it.
  • Technicals: The S&P is sitting on its 50-day average, far above its longer-term trend.
  • Sectors: Tech rose; staples, health care, banks and industrials led the declines.
  • Credit/Spreads: Lenders still charge risky companies unusually little extra yield. That leaves little cushion.
  • Crisis: Moderate stress: rising bond yields and the Gulf war are the main risks.
  • Inflation: Core inflation measures are all cooling, but price rises are still spread widely.
  • Tech Bubble: Chip valuations and easy credit look like 2000; overall valuations and investor sentiment don't.
  • Earnings & IPOs: Micron beat forecasts but slipped after hours; Oura prices its IPO this week.
  • Iran: Iran hit ships in Hormuz as Qatar-led talks stall; its oil exports rebound.
  • Warsh: The Warsh Fed hiked in September and probably leans toward one more hike.
  • Week Ahead: Next week: ISM services survey, Fed minutes, then consumer sentiment on Friday.
  • Outlook: Neutral short term. Rising yields and thin credit cushions cap the upside.
  • Trades: Favor tech over financials, trim high-yield bonds, and wait before buying gold.
  • Trades Vol: 45 watchlist names screened: 1 sell, 23 hold long, 21 stay out
  • Treasury Liquidity: Treasury liquidity/rates-vol monitor: TLT 95/100 put skew +0.60 vol pts, Fed DKW real term premium +78bp.
  • 10Y Pattern: 10Y at 100th pctile, -0bp from the 2026 rim — still compressing, not a cup-and-handle.
  • Diesel Futures: Diesel: 1-9 of 10 signals point lower.
  • Bottom line: Stocks are holding up, but bond yields are the real story. Stay selective.

The biggest story of the Wednesday Sep 30 close was the bond market, not stocks. The US 10-year Treasury yield rose 4.87bp to 5.2849% and the 30-year rose 6.28bp to 5.6286%. The 2-year rose only 1.05bp, so the curve bear-steepened: long-dated yields rose faster than short-dated ones. Meanwhile, the Bund 10Y fell 4bp to 3.586% and the JGB 10Y fell 2.9bp to 3.065%, which makes this a US-specific term-premium move rather than a global one. Stocks split along that line. The Dow fell 443.87 points (-0.86%) to 50,906.05, the S&P 500 fell 19.3 (-0.25%) to 7,651.54 and the Russell 2000 lost 0.39%. The Nasdaq Composite rose 63.52 (+0.24%) to 26,861.06 as Info Tech (+0.61%) was the only meaningful gainer. Europe was weaker: Euro Stoxx 50 -0.81%, STOXX 600 -0.50%, FTSE 100 -0.29%. The Nikkei rallied 1.94% to 66,753.72. Compared with the prior session, sentiment turned more defensive at the margin. VIX rose 0.3 to 16.34, which is still calm, and HY OAS widened 0.06 to 3.09. Energy markets stayed tense: Brent was +0.92% to 103.53 and WTI +1.16% to 90.42 after Iran hit four ships in the Strait of Hormuz, even though Iranian oil exports have recovered. After the bell, Micron beat on both EPS and revenue but traded about 1.2% lower on higher-spending commentary.

Two-sided analog episodes per signal: days where the signal's percentile-rank (vs its own full history) was <=5th or >=95th, or |z-score|>=1.3, clustered into one episode per zone per >=6-month gap between episode starts. For each zone, the realized forward 6-month % change in the BENCHMARK'S OUTRIGHT PRICE from each episode start is measured; a card's direction (BUY/SELL) is whichever sign that median historical move carries. Entry/target/stretch/stop are computed directly from this table -- the narrative prose (thesis/rationale) is the only part supplied by an LLM, and it is not permitted to alter a number. Crack spreads and curve shapes are, financially, relative-value signals rather than clean predictors of outright price; expressing every card in outright price terms is a deliberate simplification. HO36 Comdty (ULSD's 36-month point) is thin/less liquid on this seat -- treat its curve-shape reading with lower confidence than the others. Not investment advice.

Churn = the longest window of 20-120 sessions whose close range is <= 8x its median ATR(14), with median ADX(14) < 20, an insignificant close-price slope (p > 0.05), and >= 2 entries into each edge zone (top/bottom 20% of the band). Support/resistance = median swing low/high (+/-5 sessions); outer edges = the window's extreme closes. Breakout = a close beyond the outer edge by > 0.5 ATR, confirmed by a second close or one close beyond 1 ATR. A break back inside within 5 sessions is a failed break. An episode's outer edges can widen at most 0.5 ATR past their first detection, so a slow grind can't drag the range along with it. Base rates come from replaying the same rules over the full history, day by day, with no lookahead. This is pattern analysis of historical prices, not investment advice.

🔄Sector Analysis

US sectors show a narrow, growth-led market with defensives no longer providing shelter. On the day, Info Tech (+0.61%) and Cons Discr (+0.13%) were the only gainers. Cons Staples (-1.68%), Health Care (-1.39%), Industrials (-1.29%), Real Estate (-1.28%) and Financials (-1.19%) led the losses. Over one month the split is stark. Info Tech (+4.42%) and Comm Services (+4.26%) are the only positive sectors. Financials (-7.28%), Materials (-6.93%), Real Estate (-6.7%), Utilities (-6.14%) and Cons Discr (-5.91%) have been hit hard, which is consistent with rising long-end yields hurting rate-sensitive and value/cyclical groups. Year to date, Energy (+34.62%) and Info Tech (+27.79%) dominate, while Utilities (-8.73%), Cons Discr (-5.21%) and Financials (-2.74%) lag. Global sectors echo this: Info Tech +4.98% over 1m and +34.83% YTD, against Materials -6.88% and Real Estate -5.33% over 1m. Global Energy is -4.04% over 1m despite high oil. Net read: growth beats value, and both cyclicals and bond-proxy defensives are being sold. That leaves a market dependent on one leadership group, which is fragile if tech stumbles.

All spread metrics here are computed. US IG OAS is 0.82 (0.82 percentage points), z-score -0.77 and 7th percentile. That is near its historical minimum of 0.71 and far from its maximum of 6.18, and it sits at the 0th percentile of the GFC, EuroDebt, COVID and 2022-Hike stress ranges. US HY OAS is 3.09 (+0.06 on the day), z-score -0.73 and 18th percentile, about 6% of the way into the 2022-Hike range. EUR IG is 0.91 (20th percentile) and EUR HY is 3.21 (+0.05, 24th percentile), both about 10% into the COVID range. EM USD is 1.7, z-score -1.29 and 6th percentile. Credit is priced for very little risk even as Treasury yields reach cycle highs, so all-in yields are high while the spread cushion is thin. Key levels (analyst estimate). US IG: 0.71 is the floor (historical min). A move to about 1.00-1.10 would need a sustained equity drawdown of roughly 7-10% or a funding shock in financials; the Financials sector is already -7.28% over 1m. US HY: support near 2.9-3.0. A break above about 3.5-3.75 would need oil above roughly $110 Brent from Hormuz escalation or a 10Y pushing toward about 5.5%, squeezing refinancing. HY near 4.5+ would take recession-style earnings cuts. Tightening back toward the 2.33 HY historical minimum would need falling yields and a Gulf de-escalation.

💧Treasury liquidity & rates volcomputed

US Govt Securities Liquidity Index (GVLQUSD), MOVE, Fed DKW term premium and TLT option skew, live from Bloomberg + federalreserve.gov.

Five charts tracking the mechanism Simon White laid out for why Treasury liquidity is deteriorating: rising inflation volatility feeds into a higher term premium, which steepens the curve, which raises bond vol, which shows up as worse UST market liquidity. Right now UST liquidity is at the 48th percentile of its own history (higher = worse) and the Fed's own DKW real term premium is +78bp.

Latest reading is +0.60 vol points (3th percentile of the 31 runs recorded so far). Positive means the 5%-OTM put is pricier than the at-the-money option -- the market paying up for downside-price / higher-yield insurance on long-end Treasuries.

UST liquidity index is 1.51 (48th percentile of its own 2007-present history -- 100th = worst liquidity on record), deteriorating over the past 3 months (+0.05 pts). CPI YoY volatility (2yr) is 0.49pp; the article's thesis is that rising inflation vol drags liquidity worse, which this chart is built to let you check month to month.

Real term premium is +78bp (90th percentile of its own 2007-present history), up 10bp over the trailing ~2 months. Inflation risk premium is +11bp. Fed staff's own DKW decomposition (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei) splits the rise in long yields into a policy-uncertainty component (real term premium) and an inflation-uncertainty component -- both rising is the article's read that this move isn't just a rate-expectations story.

MOVE is 110.5 (80th percentile of its own post-2007 history). The 3m10s curve is 116bp (steeper by 45bp over 3 months). The article's claim is mechanical, not just correlated -- a steeper curve gives forward rates more room to move before converging to spot, which is itself higher realized/implied vol.

MOVE and the UST liquidity index have moved together with a full-history correlation of +0.72 (both series read as 'worse' when they rise). That's the closing link in the article's chain: inflation vol -> term premium -> curve steepness -> bond vol -> liquidity.

Recreates 5 charts from Bloomberg MacroScope, 'Treasury Market Liquidity Is a Live Issue Again' (Simon White, 19-Aug-2026). TLT skew accumulates one point per report run -- Bloomberg's option-surface field is snapshot-only, not retrievable historically via the API. Term premium is the Fed's own DKW model series (D'Amico-Kim-Wei, updated Kim-Walsh-Wei), pulled directly from federalreserve.gov, not Bloomberg. Not a trading signal -- a liquidity/vol monitor only.

Retracement of the left-rim decline: 76% (needs ≥90% to pass). 10Y level that passes: 6.16% (87bp above today).
Retracement = (right rim − cup base) / (left rim − cup base) = (5.28 − 0.51) / (6.79 − 0.51) = 76%.
Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base) = 0.51 + 0.90 × (6.79 − 0.51) = 6.16%.

Same test on each trailing window: cup base = lowest close in the window, left rim = highest close before it, right rim = highest close after it. Cup complete at ≥90% retracement; above 110% the yield has run past the old high (a breakout, not a cup). No cup inside the window when its left rim is not the highest close of the 91 days before it, i.e. yields were already falling into the window. Pass level = cup base + 0.90 × (left rim − cup base).

🔥Is Inflation Persistent?

Persistence score: 55/100 — Moderately persistent but cooling at the core. Every underlying trend measure (median, trimmed-mean and sticky CPI/PCE) is flagged 'falling', and their computed percentile ranks sit mid-range, roughly the 49th to 65th percentile versus history. The headline problem is breadth and energy rather than the core. In the Dallas distribution, 28.9% of the PCE basket is rising faster than 5% (13.2% above 10% plus 15.7% at 5-10%), and flexible CPI runs at 4.94%. Core PCE at 3.00759% still sits well above target, which justifies the Fed's hawkish stance even as the core trend improves.

🫧Tech Bubble Peak Again?vs March 2000
BUBBLE RESEMBLANCE · SUPER COUNT computed
11 of 22 indicators at peak-like levels · 7 beyond 2000 — 63/100
Partially there, and uneven. On headline valuation, today is far from March 2000. Nasdaq trailing P/E of 39.07x is only 15% of the way to the 175x peak, and the Nasdaq's 8.8% stretch above its 200DMA is 18% of the 2000 extreme (both computed). The froth is concentrated in the leadership group: SOX P/E of 57.33x is 93% of the way to the peak. The Late-cycle Catalyst and Signpost dimensions look more like 2000 than the valuation ones. IG credit tightness (131%), Baa-10Y tightness (165%), NFCI loose conditions (162%) and VIX complacency (199%) have all moved past their 2000-peak equivalents, and put/call is at 97%. Commodities vs equities (200%) shows capital crowded into stocks. Missing so far: retail euphoria (AAII 11%), consumer confidence (17%), a curve inversion (64%), a PMI rollover (8% and 6%) and margin-debt mania (46%). Net: the market has 2000-style complacency in credit, volatility and financial conditions, but not a 2000-style valuation or sentiment peak. On the computed path chart the current cycle (month 47, index 244.5 from Oct-2022) runs close to the 1990-anchored dot-com path, which was still about 66 months from its peak at the same stage.

Bubble-analog — today's Nasdaq vs the dot-com cycle (two anchors)

WHY TWO START DATES?
Each line is rebased to 100 at a low the tech bull launched from, so elapsed time lines up. Oct-2022 is today's anchor — it was the prior bear-market bottom. Oct-1990 is the dot-com cycle's equivalent (its literal prior bear bottom). But 1990 predates the internet mania by ~4 years, so the second chart re-anchors the dot-com line to the 1994 reset low, just before the surge ignited, for a tighter like-for-like. Today sits very early under the strict 1990 analog, further along under the 1994 surge analog.
━ Anchored at the prior bear-market bottom (Oct-1990)   ━ today's cycle
━ Anchored at the pre-internet reset low (1994)   ━ today's cycle

Valuation marker: today's Nasdaq P/E (39x) ≈ 22% of the ~175x 2000-peak P/E.

IF THIS RHYMES WITH 2000
Nasdaq fell -78.0% peak→trough (2000-03-10 → 2002-10-09, ~31 months); it took ~15 years to reclaim the high.

Think of it as three dials. Dial one, valuation, is mostly cool, except in semiconductors, where valuations have nearly reached 2000's extremes. Micron's after-hours dip on higher spending despite a large beat is a small sign of that sensitivity. Dial two, the late-cycle catalysts, is hot in one place: credit is priced for perfection. The yield curve has not inverted and the PMIs have not rolled over, which is what historically triggers the break. Dial three, the signposts, is split: professional complacency is high (low VIX, loose financial conditions) while retail mood is sour. The analyst estimates of CAPE near 39x, market cap to GDP near 215% and top-10 concentration near 40% say the aggregate market is expensive by long-run standards. Those three figures are my estimates, not web-verified in this edition. The IPO pipeline is warming: Cerebras was reported as 2026's biggest IPO and mega-listings such as Anthropic are being discussed. That argues IPO froth is elevated but not at 1999-2000 volumes. The historical warning from the computed drawdown reference is that the 2000 peak led to a -78% fall over 31 months. The trigger to watch is credit spreads widening from these tights while the 10-year stays above 5%.

⚔️Iran War

The war is at Day 215 (GlobalSecurity, Sep 30). Iran escalated attacks on Strait of Hormuz shipping on Sep 29-30, hitting four ships, and unknown projectiles struck three tankers on Sep 29 (JINSA). On diplomacy, Iran confirmed on Sep 30 that it received Washington's response to its seven-day Hormuz proposal via Qatari mediators; the contents were not disclosed. Reporting says Qatari mediation has made little progress, with both sides unwilling to move. Treasury sanctioned 10 individuals and entities over Iranian arms procurement. Two counter-currents: Fox News reports Iranian oil exports have rebounded to their highest since the US campaign began, and US forces ended their mission in Iraq, which Iran and its allies framed as a victory. Also on Sep 30, a FlyDubai Dubai-Tel Aviv flight declared an emergency after an apparent cockpit altercation and diverted to Tabuk. Market read (analyst): shipping attacks keep a risk premium in Brent (103.53), but rebounding Iranian flows and live diplomacy cap the upside unless the strait is actually closed.

🏦Fed Chair Warsh
NEAR TERM

Lean hike, 25bp, at the next FOMC meeting (inference). The Committee raised the target range by 25bp to 3.75-4.00% on Sep 16, citing elevated inflation and a 'timelier return' to 2%. iShares' baseline is one more hike in 2026. Core PCE at 3.00759% supports that. The main argument against is the falling core-trend measures.

~1 YEAR

Hold near a low-4% policy rate (inference). The September dot plot shows a low-4% fed funds rate for year-end 2026 and 2027, which implies a peak around one more hike, then an extended hold rather than cuts. Consistent with his Jackson Hole call for a 'quieter' Fed, expect less forward guidance and more data-dependence. His long-held preference for a smaller balance sheet is my inference from his prior writings and is not confirmed in this edition's sources.

Warsh has framed inflation as the primary risk. At Jackson Hole (Aug 28) he expressed concern about inflation and argued for a 'quieter' central bank with less signaling, and markets then priced a September hike, which was delivered (Sep 16 press conference). The inference: a Warsh Fed tolerates higher long-end yields as part of tightening financial conditions. That makes a policy put against the current 5.2849% 10-year unlikely unless credit or funding markets crack. Flag: the one-year path is extrapolated from the dot plot and his on-record statements, not from explicit guidance.
